findings.description: The D-7.2 gate previously required every row's registration_sha256 to equal sha256(REGISTRATION.json). registration_chain() now appends the current registration's `supersedes` value to `chain` (line 469) BEFORE checking whether any REGISTRATION*.json beside it hashes to that value; when it does not, the value is merely listed as `unresolved` and stays in the chain. validate_registration() then builds the accepted set as set(chain) (line 493), so rows whose registration_sha256 equals an unresolvable predecessor pass validation even though no registration with that content exists to inspect. `supersedes` is never checked to be a 64-hex sha256, so any non-empty string placed in the current REGISTRATION.json's `supersedes` field whitelists every row stamped with that string. Those rows are then analysed under the current registration's seed, groups, boundary_constant and sensitivities with no way to confirm the predecessor's rules were compatible; the only trace is the `unresolved_predecessor` note in the provenance block.
findings.failure_mode: A mis-authored or edited registration (or a row writer stamping an arbitrary hash) passes the pre-output validation that D-7.5 relies on; a report labelled as registered includes rows whose governing registration cannot be verified, defeating the binding the hash check exists to enforce.
findings.suggested_fix: Treat an unresolved `supersedes` as a hard InputError in validate_registration (accept only predecessors whose bytes actually hash to the declared value), or gate acceptance behind an explicit flag that is itself recorded in the output. Validate `supersedes` against ^[0-9a-f]{64}$ before following it, and keep the unresolved value out of the accepted set even if it stays in the reported lineage.

findings.cross_file_justification: The new defect-descriptions.py output is consumed by judge-sample.sh via --descriptions (judge-sample.bats JS-17/JS-19 in this diff). JS-11 documents that judge-sample.sh never exempts batch names or run ids even when the PR fixture carries them, whereas leaks() in defect-descriptions.py exempts every --forbid token on a PR-native substring match, so the two blinding filters disagree.
findings.description: leaks() exempts any detected token, including --forbid tokens intended for batch names and run ids, whenever the token appears as a plain substring anywhere in the fixture's PR.md, head.diff, head/ or base/ content (line 124: `t not in native`). The test is case-sensitive and has no word boundaries, so a short forbid token such as a batch name 'b1' is exempted by any incidental occurrence (a hex run in head.diff, part of a longer identifier). judge-sample.sh's rule for the same packets never exempts batch names or run ids, so a provenance token the operator explicitly forbade can be written into defect-descriptions.json by this tool and blinding then depends solely on the downstream filter catching it.
findings.failure_mode: A batch name or run id that happens to occur in fixture content is written into the judge-facing description file; if the downstream judge-sample.sh check is bypassed or differs in token set, the blind judge sees provenance.
findings.suggested_fix: Never exempt --forbid tokens (mirror judge-sample.sh's rule); for regex-detected arm/trial/arm tokens require a whole-token match (word-boundary regex over the PR content) or a verbatim whole-line match rather than a bare substring test.
